title: What am I? Awakening to the Question of Being
speaker: Anita Feng
summary: Anita Feng takes up the question "What am I?" as a hwado, a Korean Zen question kept alive by broad, spacious don't-know mind together with close attention to the fleeting present. Anita reads the Blue Cliff Record kongan in which Matsu, asked about his health, answers "Sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha," and walks through the five skandhas with a passage from the Anattalakkhana Sutta. Along the way come the story of the shared last breath in the room as Anita's father died, and the story of telling Zen Master Seung Sahn the question was boring and being handed a mantra instead. Anita closes with Weishan's vow to be reborn as a Kao in a neighbor's yard, a picture of service, and three sitting practices: relaxing the eyelashes, centering the air around the body, and balancing the cosmos at the crown of the head.

We look very much forward to her talk: "What Am I?
Awakening to the Question of Being."
I would also like to mention that Anita has written a wonderful book by the name of Sid.
She's a wonderfully talented sculptor, and I'm very proud to own one of her sculptures.
So thank you very much, and a warm welcome to Anita Feng.
Thank you so much for having me.
I feel like I've been acquainted with your sangha for so many years now.
So many years ago I met Nomon for the first time, and I have so much cherished our exchanges, our camaraderie.
Even though we come from different traditions and have different forms, and maybe even talk stylistically somewhat differently, we are completely steeped in the same practice.
I think that as many ways as we can meet each other is all to the good of our growth and development of Zen, and of how we carry this forward in the years and generations to come.
So thank you.
That said, I'm not sure that I have very much new to offer.

I'm not sure that I have anything particularly wise to say, other than that I come in a unique time, a unique setting, gorgeous weather here in the Pacific Northwest, in the midst of wars being carried out around the world, in the midst of sufferings near and far due to the pandemic, due to any number of crises that we live with that are completely connected to this moment and this talk.
So the subject of this talk is: what am I?
It's a question that begins, many of us think, when our provisional bodies are born into this form and into this world.
As an infant, feeling our toes, playing with our toes for the first time, there is this lively, bright investigation.
What are the perimeters of my being?
What am I?
How does this being work?
What can I do?
And if I cry, will someone take care of me?
And if I laugh, will the whole world laugh with me?
My grandmother used to say that for little people there are little problems, for big people, big problems.
So the crises of an infant, if you're a young mother, may seem insurmountable and difficult.
What am I?
What are you?
It's a conundrum that's very difficult, but things get complicated, don't they?
As we go through our youth, we try on identities for size.
I am a this, this, this.
I am a that, that, that.
When they don't work, or when we are disappointed, we move on.
It becomes a kind of checkered path, a gauntlet of experimental being.
Year after year, we try on relationships, we try on environments, we try on jobs.
Loves.
Disappointments.
Until then, there's this time when we may be on our last breath.
I think of when I was with my father as he was coming to his last breath, and his breathing was so labored.
It was so much surrounded by love and fear.
What is leaving?
What is coming?
Don't know.
Don't know.
And then that last breath, in which all of us that were there noticed that we were all releasing collectively that love, that longing, that fear.
What is this?
What am I?
All of us together took a last breath.
So really, in our sangha we spent our intensive practice period looking at myths and metaphors in Buddhism.
I think the biggest metaphor, the most pervasive metaphor that we live with so continuously, is this little one-letter word, I.
What a metaphor that is.
And yet we believe that it has some fixed form, some borders, some no-go zones.
But in fact, we are utterly and thoroughly permeable.
In our tradition of Zen, Korean Zen, we work with questions a lot.
All of you know the koans, that style of question.
But there's another style of question that we work with in our tradition of Korean Buddhism, and that is the hwado.
Have any of you heard of the hwado?
Maybe not.
This is a question that is not meant to be answered.
It is not meant to be figured out, but rather it is intended to be investigated deeply.
Sometimes it's said that the way to keep a hwado, a big question, is as if you were to keep an iron ball in your gut, to keep this burning fire.
To me, this sounds a little bit unnecessarily dramatic.
I think that the quality of keeping a question alive is one of riveting attention and broad, spacious awareness.
So we can apply this to this question, what am I?
When I first started practicing Zen in the 70s, I read Suzuki Roshi's book, Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, the first book that I read in Zen.
I absolutely loved it.
I sold my house, got rid of everything, and went to the nearest Zen master, who happened to be Zen Master Sung San, our founding teacher here in Korean Buddhism.
I went and studied with him for years.
While I was there, this was the practice that he encouraged everyone to take on: what am I?
Keep this question, what am I?
Being, I don't know, the difficult student that I've always been, one day I went to him and he asked, "Do you have any questions?"
I said, "Yes, this question.
It's really boring.
It's really not very interesting.
I can't get a grip on this.
Do you have anything else for me?"
He said, "Sure."
He said, "Sure."
That's something to be aware of as a Zen student: if you open yourself up in this way and say, "Tell me what to do," watch out.
Something will be provided.
So I was provided with a mantra practice, and that was wonderful.
I loved it.
But now, all these many years later, nearly forty-plus years later, I've developed a deep love and affection for this question.
What am I?
What am I?
How is it to be accomplished?
This question, as I said earlier, we want to investigate essentially by use of two coordinates to arrive at our awakening.
The pathway of inquiry is, on one hand, the coordinate of a broad, spacious awareness around the question, not identifying any particulars.
We call this in our tradition don't-know mind, or before-thinking mind.
Our natural impulse to slap a label on our experience, to identify and separate phenomena, is so strong in us.
But in the beautiful practicality of Zen, we can practice broad, spacious awareness: before-thinking mind, or don't-know mind.
Sometimes we use a breathing mantra, which is simply that as we inhale, we inhale internally the question, what am I?
And exhale one long don't know.
Not in the sense of "I am a dummy, I can't figure this out, I don't know," but in the sense of before thinking, of releasing our stubborn inclination to know and to narrow our field of vision.
So that's one coordinate, this coordinate of broad, spacious awareness as a question, what am I?
The other coordinate is our riveting, single-minded attention onto this provisional, fleeting moment.
Your faces, so near to me in this technological miracle of Zoom; my family going about their Sunday business just beside me, behind the closed door; the birds outside the window.
These are the ways we investigate this question, what am I?
One in the absolute realm, one in the relative realm, both together, we investigate this question.
There's a kongan I'd like to read that really expresses this very succinctly, as kongans do.
Forgive me, but in my Korean Zen we say kongans rather than koans, but you know what I mean.
This is a kongan from the Blue Cliff Record.
Matsu is unwell.
Maybe some of you know of this one.
*The great Master Matsu was not well.
The temple house master was quite concerned and went to ask him, "Master, how is your venerable health today?"
Master Ma answered, "Sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha."*
In this shorthand, this poetic shorthand of Zen, the metaphors of Zen, we can appreciate these two points of the relative and the absolute in Master Ma's reply.
Sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha.
Sun-faced Buddha is a Buddha that lives for 1800 years, thereabouts.
We could just say forever.
Why not?
Moon-faced Buddha is a Buddha that lives for a day and a night, in other words a very short time: the provisional, fleeting I.
"How is your venerable health today?
How is it going?"
If somebody asks us that, we'll say, "Well, I have a headache.
I have this to do.
I have this crisis, this joy, whatever."
This is an expression of this moon-faced Buddha.
But underneath that is the ground, the infinite ground of a sun-faced Buddha.
Our usual go-to examination of what am I is related to an idea, a metaphor of being, of a being.
But I would like to frame it differently.
I know you're familiar with this framing: that the self is a process rather than a being.
By dint of process, it combines both the absolute and the relative way of being.
Sometimes I feel compelled to say there are no, and there have never been, for example, any enlightened beings.
None.
There has only ever been enlightened being, the verb, not the noun.
Nouns are suspect.
Adverbs and adjectives are entirely suspect.
But the verb, we can be that.
This challenge of being, of identity, of what am I, is met very succinctly and profoundly in the primary Buddhist teaching of the three marks of existence.
One is impermanence.
Everything is constantly changing.
In that provisional vehicle of being, there is a constant flow.
There's nothing we can hang our hat on, as much as we try, all our lives.
Somehow this line from T.S.
Eliot comes to mind: *I grow old, I grow old, I shall wear the bottoms of my trousers rolled.* We want to identify as something, and even in our despair we still want to identify as something.
But it's all impermanence.
It's all flux.
It's all flow.
Attaining that, we attain the second mark of existence, which is non-self.
Non-self.
It's a very hard one intellectually, cognitively, to grasp.
But when we carry that balance of absolute and relative together, the provisional with the absolute, then we can taste that.
We can see that non-being.
And then by default, we are already in residence with the third mark of existence, nirvana.
So these three separate items are really not separate items.
They are one entirely.
As a practice application, and as a craftsperson, as someone who works with her hands, I like to think of Zen as being entirely practical.
So, practice.
We can practice this investigation as a question in terms of how we could, maybe every now and then on an email, tally up how many times you've used the word I.
Have you ever done that?
It's a very interesting exercise, just practicing deleting most of them.
You find there's a very interesting change of quality.

Maybe I'm speaking now more as a poet than a potter, but still there is this way in which we are so habituated to our separateness, to our idea of separateness, that if we just experiment even grammatically with this word, we can apprehend a taste of this integration of being and discover a new kind of freedom of I.

Along with that is the ongoing exploration of our willingness to change what we take, without thinking, as our I-ness: see what we hold on to and what we identify as, and open it up or hold it lightly.
Buddhism teaches us that the self is this shape-shifting and yet functional bundle of parts, the five skandhas that we just recited in the Heart Sutra.
Forms, feelings, perceptions, impulses, consciousness: the five functions or aspects that can constitute the sentient being.
In our grab bag, our gossamer, thin skin, the five skandhas are at work.
Form.
How many life forms are within this one form that we provisionally call I?
How many?
All of them being born, living out their lives, competing for space, for air, for life, killing each other off and being reborn again and again.
How many?
A lot.
I've read about it and I forget the figures almost immediately, but we know it's a lot.
Sensation, feeling.
In Buddhism, I find this very interesting: feelings, as they were categorized in early Buddhism, were only categorized in three forms.
Most of you are probably aware of this.
Either favorable, unfavorable, or neutral.
That's it.
That's it.
And all these many years later, how many words do we have to describe our feelings?
Ten thousand.

So this can be another interesting practice point: to take a step back from the categorizing and the labeling of our experience and just open it up that much, to just say unfavorable, neutral, favorable, and leave it at that.
I think you can even sense that there is an opportunity to relax and rest in openness to the totality of just that.
It's enough.
It's okay.
Naming, identifying, steering away from going down that rabbit hole of labeling our experience.
Impulses: all those habits, thoughts, ideas, opinions, prejudices, compulsions, and decisions triggered by a perception.
And finally, consciousness, the pure ground of our experience.
Consciousness, like light, has two dimensions.
Just as light can be described as both a wave and a particle, consciousness has an unbound wave or sky-like nature, the absolute world.
And it also has a particular, particle-like nature, the relative world.
I'll read a brief quote from the, I'm sure I'm not going to pronounce this right, Anata Vakana Sutra.
*The Buddha said, "The body, oh monks, is not the self.
Sensation is not the self.
Perception is not the self.
The constructions are not the self, and neither is consciousness the self.
Perceiving this, oh monks, the disciple sets no value on the body, or on sensation, or on perception, or on mental constructions, or on consciousness.
Setting no value on them, he becomes free of passions, and he is liberated.

The knowledge of liberation arises within him, and then he knows that he has done what has to be done, that he has lived the holy life, that he is no longer becoming this or that, that his rebirth is destroyed."*
Dukkha, or suffering, arises when one only identifies with or clings to one of these aggregates, skandhas.
Suffering is extinguished by releasing our grasp on them.
I find that I gravitate more towards a way of phrasing it as just holding them lightly.
We are forever human beings in the provisional world, so we have to be careful not to negate our experience and our lived problems.
But we can hold them lightly, with an open hand, so that there is the possibility always for freedom and flux and flow to occur.
I don't want to talk too long, mainly because I don't like to talk at all.
I would like to just add a few more comments, and one is to ask the question: why ask the question, what am I?
Why is this important?
Is this just a question for monks and nuns, for people who are isolated from the troubles of the world, or from just idle curiosity?
It's not that.
Not that at all.
There is this critical need for inquiry, I feel, in apprehending our responsibility.
Because what happens when we investigate this question, what am I?
We discover, again, as I said earlier, that absolute permeability of being.
If we can access that and live that, then there's no separation between self and other, between the war in Ethiopia and the people dying in India of Covid, and cooking lunch in the next room.
So our ability to be open, to access and embody impermanence, non-self and nirvana, has a job, is doing its job: saving all beings from suffering.
I'd like to refer to one other kongan, if I may.
This is called Weishan's Kao, and this is an early Chinese kongan.
*Zen Master Zheng Kong once gave the following Dharma speech: "Everything has Buddha nature, but Buddha nature is originally empty.
So how then can everything have Buddha nature?"
His assembly of monks was silent.*
This happens over and over again in every single Zen story.
They're stumped.
So now the job is on us.
*He waited, Zen Master Zheng Kong waited, and then continued: "A long time ago, the famous Zen Master Weishan said, 'When I die, I will be reborn as a Kao in the herd at my layman's house.'"*
Here again we have the shorthand, the poetry of the history of Zen.
I will be reborn as a Kao in my neighbor's yard.
It took some digging on my part, but I found an old folk reference point in this story: when someone dies, inevitably there is still a debt to be paid.
There is a responsibility to be carried out.
To be a Kao in the neighbor's yard is to provide a life source, to provide some help for those that remain, the ones that are left behind.
So whatever we create in our minds as I, it will come and go.
It will be born and it will die.
But always at the forefront of our consciousness is this responsibility to inquire: how may I help you?
How may I be of service now and forevermore?
I'll end with just one last collection of practical practice points around this question of what am I.
When you are sitting in meditation, practice relaxing your eyelashes.
This is a very gentle, easy way to tease open what we perceive to be the border of self and other, of living and death.
See what that feels like.
I think you will be surprised that you feel it.
Relax your eyelashes.
Another practice point that you could try out, for science: we are so egocentric, and this is not a judgment call, it's just our way of being.
We can tease open our idea of self in this way.
When you're seated on a cushion, practice balancing, practice centering the air that surrounds you.
See what that feels like.
And finally, the third practice point.
When you are seated in meditation, spine straight, centered in the air around you, balance the cosmos at the crown of your head.
It's easy.
It's not hard.
So with that, I would like to wish you a good question for 10,000 years, nonstop.
By investigating that question, it is my hope that we will all be liberated together.
Thank you for listening to these collections of words.
And if there are any questions or commentaries, I would enjoy that.
